newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS - Australian imports leave room for rate cut.
newsitem.headline: RTRS - Australian imports leave room for rate cut.

text.p: A small rise in Australia's imports bill for the month of August points to underlying softness in the economy that leaves the door open for another cut in interest rates this year, economists said on Wednesday.
It also suggested that markets could expect a favourable current account deficit in August, they said.
Merchandise imports rose by 1.1 percent in August, the first rise since April, the Australian Bureau of Statistics said.
Within the total rise, consumption goods were up 7.9 percent, capital goods rose 4.3 percent while intermediate goods fell 4.0 percent.

"The big story for us is that imports remain soft, it's a reflection of a soft economy, and we think the Reserve Bank will have to move on monetary policy before Christmas just to get the place going again," State Bank of New South Wales chief economist Hans Kunnen said.
Imports are one measure of demand, and so economists said the signs of continuing weakness in the series suggested that that the economy remained soft.

"It still leaves the door still open for another cut in interest rates if the economy's growth rate continues to run below potential between now and the end of the year, which is what these numbers today tend to suggest," ANZ Bank senior Treasury economist David de Garis said.
While imports rose in August, economists said the fact they rose by less than the value of an aircraft valued at A$96 million reflected underlying softness in the series.
"They were a bit softer than I thought they would be," UBS Australia chief economist Stephen Roberts said.
"I was looking for a bit more of a rebound, especially after the weakness we have seen in recent months," Roberts said.
Imports have now only risen twice in the last six months, and the August level was 7.7 percent below their level of February, their highest point this year.

Economists remained concerned about the weakness seen in capital goods. While the inclusion of the aircraft saw them rise in the month, capital goods have fallen over 18 percent in the last three months.
"Of greatest concern is the weakness in imports of capital goods," said Nomura Research senior economist Andrew Pease.
The government has forecast business investment to grow by 14 percent in the fiscal year to June 30, 1997.
While investment expectations surveys suggest that the forecast is on target, capital good imports are also seen as an indicator of business investment.
The investment forecast is seen as underpinning the government's 3.5 percent growth forecast, so any signs of weakness would be a concern to the market, economists said.
"There will need to be a substantial rebound in capital goods imports if the government's Budget forecast is to be met," Pease said.

Following the data, initial forecasts for the current account deficit for August ranged from A$1.2 billion to A$1.4 billion. Economists said such a result would be well received as it would confirm that the current account is under control and off the markets' worry list when it is released on September 30.
The current account deficit fell from over A$2 billion in May to A$1.2 billion in June, its lowest level in over two years, and was only slightly above that point in July.
In that time the fall in imports has seen the trade balance move into surplus in June and July, the first time it had been in surplus in consecutive months since early 1994.
